page: Amazon Web Services r8ib.12xlarge is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine running on the AWS Nitro System. Powered by Intel processors operating at a clock speed of 3.9 GHz, the instance delivers 48 dedicated vCPUs distributed across 24 physical cores with multithreading active at two threads per core. The instance provides 384.0 GB of system memory, establishing an allocation ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU.

Hardware configurations exclude discrete graphics accelerators and onboard ephemeral disks, offering zero GPUs and no local block storage. Workloads rely completely on network-attached storage solutions. Host communications and remote storage traffic are accommodated by a 50 Gbps baseline network bandwidth, sustaining high throughput for inter-node clustering and remote storage volumes.

The instance design emphasizes high memory capacity per core over local physical storage density. The primary tradeoff lies in the absence of local NVMe storage, shifting disk I/O demands entirely to the network layer. This architecture provides an optimal resource distribution for memory-bound workloads, such as in-memory databases, large caching layers, distributed analytics, and enterprise data processing systems.
description: Amazon Web Services r8ib.12xlarge is a memory-optimized cloud instance powered by the AWS Nitro System and 3.9 GHz Intel processors based on the x86_64 architecture. The platform features 48 dedicated virtual CPUs across 24 physical cores and supplies 384.0 GB of system RAM, providing an 8.0 GB memory-to-vCPU ratio. This configuration includes no discrete graphics processing units and features no integrated local storage, requiring network-attached storage architectures for persistence. Network performance is anchored by a 50 Gbps baseline bandwidth, delivering high-speed connectivity for multi-node clustering and decoupled volume traffic. With its substantial memory density and dedicated compute resources, r8ib.12xlarge is engineered to support memory-heavy applications, including in-memory databases, Redis or Memcached distributed clusters, in-memory analytics frameworks, and enterprise-grade enterprise resource planning backends requiring high RAM without local physical drive overhead.
